title: My first AI-built game turned into complete slop. I shipped it, then took it down
author: MakingSoulStudio
selftext:
Planning matters so much when you make a game or an app. If you start with "let's just build it and see" without deciding what the game actually is, it wanders off like mine did.



Since I started vibe coding I had this one project, a slime raising game. The idea was simple: wouldn't it be fun to watch a cute slime grow?



Then I wanted to take it on walks. Then give it a room. Then add minigames. Then contests. Then a collection book for the fish, insects and birds you get from contests. Then an ecological park for everything in the book.



Along the way, I threw away roughly 17,000 images. I built both manual walks and auto walks, then scrapped manual. I lost a huge amount of time making 30 minigames for the walks. 11 contests turned out to be about the same as making 11 more games.



Eventually I realized I didn't know what game this was anymore. And then it hit me: this isn't fun.



I was ready to let it go, but all those tokens... So I told Codex: "Do only the bare minimum verification needed to release, and ship it."



Why ship slop? So people could see what happens when you make a game badly with AI.



The first release was 3GB. Three gigabytes. I got it down to 1.2GB because I felt bad. It was Android only, and some features didn't even work, like the wardrobe. It's gone now.



That's what a game looks like when it loses its direction.



(Solo dev from Korea, translated with AI.)

comments.author: samurai_a_cat
comments.body: Congratulations, you've learned how to be a meat proxy from the experience of this project. Now you can study game design and become an engineer.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Yeah, I'll use this as a chance to study hard.

replies.author: samurai_a_cat
replies.body: Good luck with that. And try to keep control of the project. Remember that in a team with LLMs, your first priority is to be the technical leader and the main game designer. And not just "asking for ideas to be implemented."

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Thanks for the advice. This was the moment I really learned that the hard way: AI is just a tool for making my game.

comments.author: DealerIcy3439
comments.body: I have the idea, just is a headache to manage. It was planned before I started

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Rooting for you to make that idea real. Let's both keep at it!

comments.author: max13007
comments.body:
My first game was similar. Just an incremental game I dropped onto Itch to test the waters. It taught me a lot about how quickly a project can become unmanageable, and how quickly I can lose the passion and vision once I start letting the AI make choices for me. 

The game came out fine, it's entertaining and those I've asked to try it seem to like it, but I don't feel very attached to it. 

My approach has shifted drastically for the project I'm working on now. I expect to not release this for a long time, if I ever even do.

replies.author: MVPof93
replies.body:
This is really interesting because I am going through it too right now. Too many ideas and I love them all, then I let AI make decisions and start losing passion quickly. I think I need to go back to making decisions on them again. 

To add as well, this is all new for me. Learning as we go!

replies.author: max13007
replies.body:
Right there with you! It's dazzling to see our ideas come to life, and sobering to be reminded how hard it is to build something good. 

I'm already expecting that I may need to start from scratch on my ideas. But each time I restart, I'll get better and better, as too will the end product. 

Rootin' for ya! We'll get there

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: AI has definitely lowered the technical barrier, but I think there are still things only people can do, like planning, thinking it through, and polishing. I'm learning that through a lot of trial and error.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Same here. After that experience, I'm trying to only release things that I honestly feel are fun or that I think are really good ideas.

replies.author: max13007
replies.body: Same! If/when I do release my next project, I'll be sure it's truly mine.

comments.author: Stinky_You
comments.body: Excellent PSA. This is what I'm currently trying to avoid, working on 3D with no experience. I've downsized the project once already to make the scope more realistic for me. Avoiding putting together a piece of garbage means everything needs attention, claudecode is waaaay to trigger happy (ready to build) when I'm giving examples during a brainstorm

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Right, and if you don't set rules for when brainstorming kicks in, it can even start brainstorming over small bug fixes and burn a ton of tokens. Speaking from experience ㅠㅠ

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body:
There's nothing wrong with building in an experimental way, but you have to have a period of consolidation where you trim back to the essentials and make all parts of the game function as a coherent whole. If you just keep doing, "okay, but what if we add X. Cool, now add Y", eventually you are going to get a pile of shit. It's like if you mix every color of paint together, ain't going to look so pretty. 

I start my games with only a very rough idea and experiment like a mad man. Usually by about the end of the first week the mechanics and overall direction have solidified and from there it goes from prototype to production.

Anyway, no shame in a failure, I'm sure you'll do much better on the next one.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: You're right. This really made me feel how important planning is when making a game. From now on, I'm going to make better games with better planning.

replies.author: Matuflex88
replies.body: AI makes that so much easier: if i want to try out a new feature, i can do so in little time. Before i would have to think really if it would be worth spending a week+ of my time on a feature i am not sure about.

comments.author: daddy_reloaded
comments.body: Ok you got me. I want to play your game. Please

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Sadly, the time for experiencing the slop has passed, I already deleted it. I'll be back with a more finished game next time. Please play that one!

comments.author: redditisawesomee
comments.body: I could relate to you a lot. You have to understand that the incredible ability of ai makes it easy to get tunnel vision and lose track of things, because you can explore every idea you have during the building stage and you might eventually get carried away. Its only too late when you realized that the original game idea that you had has now evolved into a complex mess. Creative process is building and refining and filtering and desconstructing and redesigning. It takes a lot of time to produce a well thought out  product that can be fun and also is coherent and clear. So dont be in a rush, take your time and refine your product.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Thanks, that's good advice. Since this experience, I've been trying to get the planning solid first.

comments.author: ralkuzu
comments.body:
It's like painting Warhammer, you start off painting straight paint onto the bare plastic, it looks crap and nothing blends well

Then you learn about undercoating and priming

It looks a little better now

Then you learn dry brushing and you can't believe the magic of how easy it is to add details so fast

Then you plateau a bit, thinking hmmm, constantly try to paint details but get splotches everywhere 

Maybe even a few re coats and going through many types of different brushes to various success 

You get frustrated, look at others models and how well they look and how on earth did they make it look so great 

Then you discover oil

Holy shit the oil makes it look so great, highlights all the details and makes it have depth

You then combine this with dry brushing and finally 

You have a half decent painted model

But you forgot to file away the mould lines at the end again 


They key is keep making mistakes, keep smudging paint in the wrong places, understand it's a process of various layers and don't try to build it perfectly from square one

I've been trying myself and holy shit it's a lot to take in , balance, sounds, bugs, game play loop that's fun


It seems easy at first but wow, it really does take something to make a good game that's playable, let us keep grinding

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: The figure painting comparison really hits home, thank you. Let's keep at it and make good games together!

comments.author: ParkInsider
comments.body:
Same situation here. One advice that has stuck with me is "make sure the core loop is fun".

I have five games in progress, three of them are absolutely brilliant, fucking high concept shit, that's gonna blow people's minds... and boring as fuck.

Two of them are dumb as a rock, easy to get, easy to play, satisfying and... fun!

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: AI doesn't know what fun is. In a way, I think something simple but fun can sometimes be a much better design than just having a great idea.

replies.author: ParkInsider
replies.body: For real. It has no idea what is fun or satisfying.

comments.author: cratercamper
comments.body: Don't beat yourself down. The most important thing is that you managed to create something. 100 % of those bad mouths never built anything (otherwise they would know better - that it is HARD to build something).  I wouldn't call it AI slop even if you worked on it hard and long - just bad game. Vibecoding is LSD - so many things are happening, so many things are possible, it is easy to get carried out. Just go forward with your head up. If/when you do next game you will be much more experienced and result will be better.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Thanks for the support. This one is my failure story, but I also have games I'm happy with that I'm working hard to run. I'll keep at it. Thanks again!

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio

comments.author: Livid_Shallot5701

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio

Well, scope planning. Not the entire game. 

Next game I need to set the scope even more fleshed out than I did this time, but then stick to it religiously and not get swayed by unlimited "easy feature tests and oh now we practically made it anyway to test it, might as well  implement it" scope creep

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Really good advice, thank you!

comments.author: Electrical-Cheetah90
comments.body: I wish you had more upvotes. "Feature creep" is a real hazard of vibecoding, and I appreciate seeing posts like this that warn me of its dangers

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: I'm glad if my post helped someone. I'll keep trying to share what I go through while making games, whether it's a success or a failure.

comments.author: Daytona24
comments.body:
This is the only downside to the "AI Slop" comments.  The only thing you did wrong here is not properly play it first BEFORE you released it.  There is nothing wrong with a learning experience but when people start putting the stuff out there the good AI games etc will be treated the same way.  I myself am working on a few things. Some I consider "finished" and others are just being born.  But I'm making them for ME with the hopes of maybe putting them out there.  I guess that's my golden AI rule right now, make it for yourself and if its good enough then send it out to the world.  

Because of AI there are a lot of good ideas, games, concepts, programs and developments coming from people who have the ideas but not the proper skills to make those ideas come to life.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: You're right. I was also someone who had ideas but not the skills to make them real. Once I could finally build them, I got too greedy, never pinned down the design, and ended up with this failure. I'll use this as a lesson and make better games. Wish me luck!

replies.author: According_Cut_1956
replies.body: So right, the difference between AI slop and top tier games made by AI is just iterations and how much your willing to play and test the game.

comments.author: Alki_Soupboy
comments.body:
Kinda sounds like what I'm doing, but I keep realizing that, throwing everything out, and starting from scratch. I might actually make it fun one day.

I got a question for people that I'm curious to hear: Do you do pretty minimal graphics first and work on getting the game play elements working really well, or (like me) you tend to get the look how you want it first and then start refining the gameplay?

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: On this failed project, I built the design first, the way I wanted it to look. Now I implement the bare minimum, finish the features first, and leave the design for the polish stage. While building that minimum, I do test a few sample designs first to check they come out the way I want.

replies.author: Alki_Soupboy
replies.body: I have to get the graphics up to at least a respectable level or else it’s painful to play. Regardless, it’s a fun little hobby. If it takes me 10 years, I’ll keep slowly plugging away.  At least I’ll probably have the story locked in by then. 😂

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: I'm determined to make a game people really enjoy and have fun with too. Let's both keep at it!

comments.author: I_pee_in_shower
comments.body: The outcome doesn’t matter only what you learn from it. Take your learnings and try again or move onto something else.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: I really did learn a lot. It was a good experience.

comments.author: starwaver
comments.body:
Thank you for not shipping slop.
AI is perfectly capable of creating a good game, but is also much easier to ship slop that isn't fun.
Sadly many will ship it regardless of quality and bring a bad view to AI generated game development. As good game developers, it's more important than ever to make sure the game is fun before shipping it

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: When you decide something has failed, you have to be willing to let it go. I only want to keep running games I'm happy with myself.

comments.author: Worried_Number5115
comments.body:
You mention so many great points in this post and I think this is actually good. I don’t think you should’ve shipped a slop game but you learned how hard game dev is, even if you have the greatest tools & AI doing the coding. 

1st and foremost, the game needs to be fun, you hit the nail on the head. Without this, it’s not a game IMO. 

Instead of adding random things to scope as you build, you should create a master plan and vision and scope of of the main infrastructure and how it’s all interconnected before you ever instruct AI to code. Things will get added to the scope regardless, but your base will be strong and any addition that can’t be integrated into the existing architecture should just get scrapped. 

I’m 100% positive you’re next attempt at creating a game will be much better based on your transparent self analysis

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Thank you so much for saying that. I want to keep growing so that one day people will think, "A game made by this dev? I can trust that."

comments.author: Drunkendrakon6
comments.body:
Oh I just kept pressing on and once everything worked I just took an equal amount of time polishing the game. I think it's been in development for 5 months total not including learning and previous dev work in unity before switching to my own engine. Building games takes a lot of persistence, taste and execution. 

If you don't know what you want the AI can't possibly execute your vision.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Exactly. In the end, my game failed because I wasn't clear from the start about what I wanted to make. I learned a lot this time.

comments.author: Shrineheart
comments.body:
Sounds like a case of scope creep. You start planning a game and then you add a million features. Then the game mutates into something you don't recognize or the project becomes too big to handle.
When you start planning a game you throw all these weird cool ideas down on paper. Then you start considering how you would make it work and if it would be fun for the player. From there it's whittling things down, tinkering, and considering "what do I need for the base part of the game?".
Then it's "what can the player unlock? How do they unlock it?"
All the really cool stuff can wait until the basic stuff is set up cause you build up from the basic stuff.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: Exactly. I got greedy. I started with 1 slime type and grew it to 10, each with a different shape. I planned 2 tournaments and ended up making 11. Everything I touched ballooned in size while the quality went down. Not thinking about how I would actually build things was also a big mistake.

replies.author: Shrineheart
replies.body:
The best method (I have a really big project I'm working on too) is to focus on one thing and make it so you can reuse that thing. Once you have one slime built and working that same code can be used for the other slimes with little modification. 
I have chickens in my game. There's going to be multiple breeds. But right now I have a placeholder chicken that does the default chicken actions. Once I know what a chicken does and how it should behave all the other chickens get that same behavior.
Modifying that behavior like laying more eggs or different eggs is just additional modifiers the AI can implement.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: That's why I'm keeping the assets and minigames I made, in case they're useful for my next game. I see those as valuable assets too.

comments.author: getloadoutai
comments.body: the 17K images part made me physically wince lol. 30 minigames just for the walks is basically a second gamer except for shipping, it as a warning instead of quietly deleting it tho and what fixed this for me was writing like 3 sentences on what the game actually is before opening claude or codex, then making it check every new feature against that. doesnt serve the slime and was the walking ever fun or did the contests kill it!

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body:
I shared it as a warning, and the game itself is deleted now.



The walks were me being greedy. I should have kept them simple, but I was chasing the fun of watching, so I started building the maps in 3D and the size of the project exploded. In the end, I failed to create the fun of watching that I wanted.



With more development, the tournaments might have become somewhat fun to watch. But once I realized my game was slop, there was no point in continuing.

comments.author: NecroGoggles
comments.body: Gratz on doing something that’s more than a lot of people do. Second, I don’t understand why people think they should be amazing at something when they first starting. This is a learning experience and it sounds like that’s what’s going on. You know now kind of what works. What needs some tweaking and what next steps are. And I think you should be a little bit more forgiving think about if you could even make this a year ago the fact that you made something even if it was ““AI slop “ is pretty amazing. Next step is to figure out like everyone’s saying what a good game is like I feel like that’s totally possibilities now.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: You're right, it was a good experience. When you're learning something, even a failure like this is a valuable asset. Thanks for the encouragement, I'll try to make good games from here on.

comments.author: Ok-Protection-6612
comments.body: Scope creep is not unique to AI game dev

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: That's true. It's the same in business too. In the end, I think things only move forward once you accept that you can't fit in everything you want.

comments.author: albertsimondev
comments.body: Respect for taking it down instead of defending it. My first pass at VybeCiv (a browser 4X I'm building with AI) had the same problem: lots of systems, nothing that made a turn feel like a decision. What helped me was cutting features until every remaining one changed what the player does next turn. AI makes adding stuff free, so cutting becomes the actual design work.

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: "Lots of systems" says it all. You think you've packed in as much fun as you wanted, but it feels like all you did was make it complicated. I know that feeling too well.

comments.author: yoursissysex
comments.body: Ah, now the anti-ai-haters flood ai-subs with fictional stories to be "convincing"... 🤭

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body:
I'm someone who is very happy with how far AI has come, and grateful for it. Thanks to AI, I could step into game development, a field I could only imagine before because I didn't have the skills.



This failure hasn't made me want to give up on game dev, and I have no intention of convincing anyone of anything. I just wanted to share this experience and talk with other developers.

comments.author: SuchZookeepergame387
comments.body: failing a game is good , you did learn a lot from it soo next time you will have a better plan

replies.author: MakingSoulStudio
replies.body: You're right, I learned a lot from this failure. Thanks for the encouragement!
